claim: PARP1 is both a first responder to DNA damage and a chromatin architectural protein.
source: Poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase 1 (PARP1) is both a first responder to DNA damage and a chromatin architectural protein.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of PARP1's dual roles.

claim: PARP1 association with DNA is diffusion-limited.
source: Here, we show that PARP1 association with DNA is diffusion-limited
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of association rates presented in the manuscript.

claim: Release of PARP1 from DNA is promoted by binding of an additional DNA molecule that facilitates a 'monkey bar' mechanism.
source: release of PARP1 from DNA is promoted by binding of an additional DNA molecule that facilitates a 'monkey bar' mechanism, also known as intersegment transfer.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by kinetic experiments showing DNA-dependent DNA dissociation.

claim: The WGR-domain of PARP1 is essential to the monkey bar mechanism.
source: The WGR-domain of PARP1 is essential to this mechanism
evidence: This is supported by experiments with domain deletion mutants showing altered kinetics.

claim: A point mutation (W589A) recapitulates the altered kinetics of the WGR domain deletion.
source: a point mutation (W589A) recapitulates the altered kinetics of the domain deletion.
evidence: This is demonstrated by kinetic experiments comparing W589A mutant to ΔWGR mutant.

claim: The W589A mutant accumulates at sites of DNA damage more slowly following laser micro-irradiation than wild-type PARP1.
source: the W589A mutant accumulates at sites of DNA damage more slowly following laser micro-irradiation than wild-type PARP1.
evidence: This is supported by live cell imaging experiments showing reduced accumulation rates.

claim: Clinically relevant inhibitors of PARP1 did not alter the rate or mechanism of the release of PARP1 from DNA.
source: Clinically relevant inhibitors of PARP1 did not alter the rate or mechanism of the release of PARP1 from DNA.
evidence: This is supported by stopped-flow experiments with four different PARP inhibitors.

claim: PARP1 serves as a first responder to DNA damage.
source: Poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase 1 (PARP1) serves as a first responder to DNA damage and is the founding member and most abundant representative of the large family of diphtheria toxin-like ADP-ribosyltransferases (ARTDs) (Bai, 2015; Bock and Chang, 2016; Beck et al., 2014; Daniels et al., 2015; De Vos et al., 2012; Mashimo et al., 2014; Morales et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: PARP1 is the founding member and most abundant representative of the large family of diphtheria toxin-like ADP-ribosyltransferases (ARTDs).
source: Poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase 1 (PARP1) serves as a first responder to DNA damage and is the founding member and most abundant representative of the large family of diphtheria toxin-like ADP-ribosyltransferases (ARTDs) (Bai, 2015; Bock and Chang, 2016; Beck et al., 2014; Daniels et al., 2015; De Vos et al., 2012; Mashimo et al., 2014; Morales et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Binding to either single or double-strand DNA breaks enzymatically activates PARP1 to use NAD+ in polymerizing long chains of poly(ADP)-ribose.
source: Binding to either single or double-strand DNA breaks (SSBs or DSBs) enzymatically activates PARP1 to use NAD+ in polymerizing long chains of poly(ADP)-ribose (PAR) onto itself and other nuclear acceptor proteins such as histones and DNA repair proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PARP1 function.

claim: PAR chains recruit the appropriate DNA repair machinery containing PAR-binding motifs.
source: These PAR chains then recruit the appropriate DNA repair machinery containing PAR-binding motifs (Karlberg et al., 2013; Teloni and Altmeyer, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PARP1 is a validated target for cancer therapy.
source: PARP1 is of special interest because it is a validated target for cancer therapy (Tangutoori et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Olaparib and rucaparib are in clinical use for treatment of ovarian and/or breast cancer in BRCA1/2 negative patients.
source: Most notably, olaparib and rucaparib are in clinical use for treatment of ovarian and/or breast cancer in BRCA1/2 negative patients
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge.

claim: The 16 members of the ARTD family all share a common catalytic core domain (~40 kDa).
source: Overall, the domain structures of the 16 members of the ARTD family are quite diverse, but they all share a common catalytic core domain (~40 kDa) (Barkauskaite et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Clinically relevant inhibitors of PARP1 bind in the catalytic domain.
source: Clinically relevant inhibitors of PARP1 bind in the catalytic domain.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PARP inhibitor mechanism.

claim: The N-terminal region of PARP1 contains five additional domains: three Zn-finger domains, an automodification domain that contains a BRCT-fold, and a WGR domain.
source: The N-terminal region of PARP1 contains five additional domains; three Zn-finger domains, an automodification domain that contains a BRCT-fold, and a WGR domain (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1A showing the domain structure.

claim: Zn1, Zn2, Zn3, and the WGR domain collaborate to recognize DNA strand breaks in a structure-specific and sequence-independent manner.
source: Seminal work from the Pascal laboratory has provided a molecular understanding of how Zn1, Zn2, Zn3, and the WGR domain collaborate to recognize DNA strand breaks in a structure-specific and sequence-independent manner, and subsequently activate the catalytic activity of PARP1.
evidence: This is supported by citations to work from the Pascal laboratory.

claim: Zn1 and Zn2 separately bind one DNA end each using two points of contact, termed the phosphate backbone grip and the base stacking loop.
source: Zn1 and Zn2 separately (Langelier et al., 2011a), and together in the context of an SSB (Eustermann et al., 2015), bind one DNA end each using two points of contact, termed the phosphate backbone grip and the base stacking loop.
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: In the context of a DSB, Zn1 maintains the grip-loop interaction mode while the Zn3 and WGR domains make additional contacts to the DNA.
source: In the context of a DSB, this grip-loop interaction mode is maintained by Zn1, while the Zn3 and WGR domains make additional contacts to the DNA (Figure 1B) (Langelier et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural study and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Stepwise assembly of the different domains of PARP1 on DNA leads to the destabilization of the helical subdomain (HD) of the catalytic domain, which results in activation of its ADP-ribosyl transferase activity.
source: Importantly, stepwise assembly of the different domains of PARP1 on DNA leads to the destabilization of the helical subdomain (HD) of the catalytic domain, which results in activation of its ADP-ribosyl transferase activity (Eustermann et al., 2015; Langelier et al., 2018; Dawicki-McKenna et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: PARP1 contributes to many types of DNA repair mechanisms, including base excision repair, homologous recombination, nucleotide excision repair, and alternative non-homologous end-joining.
source: In cells, PARP1 is known to contribute to many types of DNA repair mechanisms, including base excision repair, homologous recombination, nucleotide excision repair, and alternative non-homologous end-joining (de Murcia et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In vitro, PARP1 is activated by a wide variety of DNA damage models including nicks, gaps, blunt ends, 5'- or 3'- extensions, all with or without a 5'-phosphate.
source: In vitro, PARP1 is activated by a wide variety of DNA damage models including nicks, gaps, blunt ends, 5'- or 3'- extensions, all with or without a 5'-phosphate (Langelier et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: PARP1 binds tightly to undamaged DNA.
source: There is now clear evidence from multiple laboratories that PARP1 also binds tightly to undamaged DNA.
evidence: This is supported by multiple lines of evidence cited in the manuscript.

claim: PARP1 binds to and condenses intact chromatin, represses Pol II-dependent transcription, and is activated for auto-PARylation.
source: For example, the Kraus laboratory has shown that PARP1 binds to and condenses intact chromatin, represses Pol II-dependent transcription, and is activated for auto-PARylation (Kim et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to work from the Kraus laboratory.

claim: PARP1 serves as a chromatin architectural protein and interacts tightly (Kd ~nM) with and is activated by various nucleosome constructs.
source: We have previously shown that PARP1 serves as a chromatin architectural protein and interacts tightly (Kd ~nM) with and is activated by various nucleosome constructs (Clark et al., 2012; Muthurajan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work from the authors' laboratory.

claim: Atomic force microscopy has shown that PARP1 binds not only to DNA ends or specific nicks, but also has significant affinity for undamaged DNA.
source: Additionally, atomic force microscopy has shown that PARP1 binds not only to DNA ends or specific nicks, but also has significant affinity for undamaged DNA (Sukhanova et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Single molecule tightrope assays have demonstrated that PARP1 interacts with and moves along undamaged DNA.
source: Most recently, single molecule tightrope assays have demonstrated that PARP1 interacts with and moves along undamaged DNA (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: PARP1 significantly accumulates at DNA damage sites in less than 10 s following laser micro-irradiation in live cells.
source: In fact, laser micro-irradiation experiments in live cells have shown that PARP1 significantly accumulates at DNA damage sites in less than 10 s (Mortusewicz et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: DNA concentrations in the nucleus are ~100 mg/mL.
source: PARP1 must rapidly search the genome for damaged DNA, yet it has significant affinity for the billions of base pairs of undamaged DNA that are present at concentrations of ~100 mg/mL in the nucleus (Krebs et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Some localized sliding along DNA has been reported for PARP1.
source: While some localized sliding along DNA has been reported for PARP1 (Liu et al., 2017), a more thorough kinetic characterization of binding to and dissociation from DNA is needed in order to address how PARP1 can efficiently localize to sites of DNA damage to initiate repair.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: PARP1 has been found to associate more tightly with DNA in vivo in the presence of clinically relevant inhibitors, a phenomenon known as PARP 'trapping'.
source: PARP1 has been found to associate more tightly with DNA in vivo in the presence of clinically relevant inhibitors. This phenomenon, known as PARP 'trapping' (Tangutoori et al., 2015; Brown et al., 2016; Shen et al., 2015; Murai et al., 2012; Pommier et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PARP trapping is thought to be in part responsible for the clinical effects of PARP inhibitors.
source: This phenomenon, known as PARP 'trapping' (Tangutoori et al., 2015; Brown et al., 2016; Shen et al., 2015; Murai et al., 2012; Pommier et al., 2016) is thought to be in part responsible for the clinical effects of PARP inhibitors
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Talazoparib is 100-fold more potent at trapping PARP1 on DNA and >50 fold more potent at killing cancer cells than rucaparib and olaparib.
source: For example, talazoparib is 100-fold more potent at trapping PARP1 on DNA and >50 fold more potent at killing cancer cells than rucaparib and olaparib, although the apparent IC-50's for all three compounds are quite similar (1–5 nM) (Shen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The apparent IC-50's for talazoparib, rucaparib, and olaparib are quite similar (1–5 nM).
source: For example, talazoparib is 100-fold more potent at trapping PARP1 on DNA and >50 fold more potent at killing cancer cells than rucaparib and olaparib, although the apparent IC-50's for all three compounds are quite similar (1–5 nM) (Shen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Extensive biochemical investigations of PARP1 trapping failed to provide evidence for an allosteric interaction between DNA- and inhibitor-binding.
source: Further complicating matters, extensive biochemical investigations of PARP1 trapping failed to provide evidence for an allosteric interaction between DNA- and inhibitor-binding (Hopkins et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Trapping is due solely to inhibition of catalytic activity.
source: extensive biochemical investigations of PARP1 trapping failed to provide evidence for an allosteric interaction between DNA- and inhibitor-binding (Hopkins et al., 2015), suggesting that trapping is due solely to inhibition of catalytic activity (but see [Langelier et al., 2018]).
evidence: This is an inference from prior literature with a caveat citation.

claim: The rate of association of PARP1 with DNA (k1) is 3.1 nM−1s−1.
source: Our analysis yields a k1 of 3.1 nM−1s−1 (Scheme 1, Table 1)
evidence: This is derived from stopped-flow experiments and global fitting analysis.

claim: The rate of association of PARP1 with DNA is significantly greater than previously reported using surface plasmon resonance.
source: Our analysis yields a k1 of 3.1 nM−1s−1 (Scheme 1, Table 1), which is significantly greater than previously reported for PARP1 associating with DNA as measured using surface plasmon resonance (Jorgensen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior literature.

claim: The upper bound for k-1 (dissociation rate constant) is 10 s−1.
source: Using global fitting, we could derive an upper bound for k-1 of 10 s−1.
evidence: This is derived from global fitting analysis of experimental data.

claim: The true equilibrium dissociation constant (KD) of a double-strand break under these conditions is <3 nM.
source: Thus, the true equilibrium dissociation constant (KD) of a double-strand break under these conditions is <3 nM (Figure 4—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is calculated from the kinetic rate constants.

claim: The KD of <3 nM is lower than previously reported KDs of 31 nM, 14 nM, and 97 nM.
source: Thus, the true equilibrium dissociation constant (KD) of a double-strand break under these conditions is <3 nM (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), lower than the previously reported KDs of 31 nM (Clark et al., 2012), 14 nM (Langelier et al., 2010), and 97 nM (Langelier et al., 2018)
evidence: This is a comparison to prior literature.

claim: Unlabeled p18mer behaves similarly to fluorescein labeled p18mer* in the assay.
source: We began these investigations by first performing a label-swap experiment to ensure that unlabeled p18mer behaves similarly to fluorescein labeled p18mer*.
evidence: This is demonstrated by label-swap experiments.

claim: kobs increases at increasing concentrations of competitor DNA.
source: However, as seen in the data in Figure 3 by comparing dissociation in the presence of 2.2 vs 4 µM DNA, and in the replot of kobs vs. multiple concentrations of competitor DNA, kobs increases at increasing concentrations of competitor DNA (Figure 3, inset).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Attempts to fit the dissociation data with Scheme 2 in Kintek Explorer yielded very poor fits and highly skewed residuals.
source: Additionally, attempts to fit these data with Scheme 2 in Kintek Explorer yielded very poor fits and highly skewed residuals (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by fitting analysis.

claim: Competitor DNA is actively contributing to the dissociation of the pre-bound p18mer*.
source: Thus, a different kinetic scheme is needed to fit these data, one where competitor DNA is actively contributing to the dissociation of the pre-bound p18mer*.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic data and fitting analysis.

claim: The simplest model to explain active participation of a competitor DNA in the dissociation of an already bound DNA is formation of a ternary complex wherein the competing DNA binds to PARP1 prior to the dissociation of the pre-bound DNA.
source: The simplest model to explain active participation of a competitor DNA in the dissociation of an already bound DNA is formation of a ternary complex wherein the competing DNA binds to PARP1 prior to the dissociation of the pre-bound DNA (Scheme 3).
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed to explain the data.

claim: The quality of the fits with the kinetic model in Scheme 3 provides strong support for the requisite formation of a ternary complex in the dissociation of DNA from PARP1.
source: The quality of the fits with the kinetic model in Scheme 3 provides strong support for the requisite formation of a ternary complex in the dissociation of DNA from PARP1.
evidence: This is supported by the good fits of the data to the model.

claim: The second order rate constant of association for the second DNA molecule is 0.043 nM−1s−1, almost two orders of magnitude lower than that for association of the first DNA oligomer.
source: The second order rate constant of association for the second DNA molecule is 0.043 nM−1s−1 is almost two orders of magnitude lower than that for association of the first DNA oligomer.
evidence: This is derived from global fitting of kinetic data.

claim: The KD for the second DNA strand is 2600 nM.
source: The KD for the second DNA strand is 2600 nM, explaining why this complex would be rarely if ever detected under typical experimental conditions performed at nanomolar concentrations of PARP1.
evidence: This is calculated from the kinetic rate constants.

claim: The rates of association and dissociation for the second DNA are not 'symmetrical'.
source: Note that the rates of association and dissociation for the second DNA are not 'symmetrical' (i.e. k2 ≠ k-3 and k-2 ≠ k3).
evidence: This is observed from the kinetic parameters in Table 1.

claim: The pre-bound DNA is less likely to dissociate than the second competitor DNA.
source: This asymmetry is most pronounced in the comparison between k-2 and k3: the pre-bound DNA is less likely to dissociate than the second competitor DNA.
evidence: This is observed from the kinetic parameters.

claim: The newly incoming DNA presumably binds to a different (weaker) site than the originally more tightly bound DNA.
source: This observation makes intuitive sense in that the newly incoming DNA presumably binds to a different (weaker) site than the originally more tightly bound DNA.
evidence: This is an inference from the kinetic data.

claim: The kinetically derived dissociation constants (KDs) for the two DNA binding sites are quite similar.
source: Although there is a lack of symmetry in the rate constants, the kinetically derived dissociation constants (KDs) are quite similar (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Formation of a ternary complex with two different DNA molecules bound simultaneously requires two separate DNA binding sites.
source: Formation of a ternary complex with two different DNA molecules bound simultaneously requires two separate DNA binding sites.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the ternary complex model.

claim: PARP1 has four domains that are known to contribute to DNA binding: Zn1, Zn2, Zn3, and WGR.
source: PARP1 has four domains that are known to contribute to DNA binding: Zn1, Zn2, Zn3, and WGR (Figure 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge shown in Figure 1.

claim: Zn1, Zn3, and WGR are essential for catalytic activity.
source: As previously reported (Langelier et al., 2012), Zn1, Zn3, and WGR are essential for catalytic activity, and thus deletion of these domains disrupts PARylation activity.
evidence: This is supported by citation and confirmed by activity assays.

claim: Deletion of the non-essential Zn2 domain does not affect PARylation activity.
source: On the other hand, the deletion of the non-essential Zn2 domain does not affect PARylation activity.
evidence: This is shown by activity assays in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: All four domain deletion constructs bound to DNA with similar second-order rate constants (k1s) despite each missing one DNA-binding domain.
source: Despite each construct missing one DNA-binding domain, all four bound to DNA with similar second-order rate constants (k1s, Table 1, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–4).
evidence: This is shown by stopped-flow experiments with domain deletion mutants.

claim: The Zn deletions (ΔZn1, ΔZn2, and ΔZn3) behaved essentially like wild-type PARP1 in the dissociation experiment.
source: In the dissociation experiment, the Zn deletions (ΔZn1, ΔZn2, and ΔZn3) behaved essentially like wild-type PARP1: increasing competitor DNA concentrations yielded increasing kobs, and the data were best described by global fitting of the kinetic model of Scheme 3 with the formation of a ternary complex (Figure 4—figure supplements 3–5, Table 1).
evidence: This is shown by dissociation experiments with domain deletion mutants.

claim: The ΔWGR mutant behaved dramatically differently from wild-type: increasing concentrations of competitor DNA did not yield higher kobss.
source: In contrast, the ΔWGR mutant behaved dramatically differently; increasing concentrations of competitor DNA did not yield higher kobss, and globally the data were best described by Scheme 2 (Figure 5A, Table 1).
evidence: This is shown by dissociation experiments with the ΔWGR mutant.

claim: In the structure of PARP1 bound to a DSB, Trp589 in the WGR domain stacks against the ribose sugar of the 5'-end of the DNA.
source: In the structure of PARP1 bound to a DSB, Trp589 in the WGR domain stacks against the ribose sugar of the 5'-end of the DNA (Figure 1) (Langelier et al., 2012).
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure cited and depicted in Figure 1.

claim: The W589A point mutation is properly folded, as the mutant and wild-type PARP1 have identical melting temperatures (43.9 ± 0.3 vs. 43.3 ± 0.3°C).
source: The W589A point mutation is properly folded, as the mutant and wild-type PARP1 have identical melting temperatures (43.9 ± 0.3 vs. 43.3 ± 0.3°C).
evidence: This is shown by thermal stability measurements.

claim: The W589A mutant bound to free DNA rapidly.
source: Similar to what was observed with the deletion of the entire WGR domain, the W589A mutant also bound to free DNA rapidly (Figure 2—figure supplement 5)
evidence: This is shown by association experiments.

claim: The W589A mutant released DNA via the simple mechanism in Scheme 2 that is not dependent on binding a second DNA molecule.
source: the W589A mutant also bound to free DNA rapidly (Figure 2—figure supplement 5), and released DNA via the simple mechanism in Scheme 2 that is not dependent on binding a second DNA molecule (Figure 5B, Table 1).
evidence: This is shown by dissociation experiments.

claim: Intact plasmid (4.5 kb; ~90% supercoiled and 10% nicked) at 5 nM is a surprisingly effective competitor of a pre-formed 25 nM complex.
source: Intact plasmid (4.5 kb;~90% supercoiled and 10% nicked) at 5 nM is a surprisingly effective competitor of a pre-formed 25 nM complex, yielding a kobs comparable to what is observed with 1 µM p18mer (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown by competition experiments with plasmid DNA.

claim: 5 nM of p18mer yields no observable release of p18mer.
source: For comparison, 5 nM of p18mer yields no observable release of p18mer (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown by competition experiments.

claim: Undamaged DNA is an effective trigger for the release of pre-bound p18mer*.
source: These results demonstrate that undamaged DNA is an effective trigger for the release of pre-bound p18mer*.
evidence: This is concluded from the plasmid competition experiments.

claim: The observed kobs is unchanged regardless of whether the concentration of ends is 10 nM (cut once), 20 nM (cut twice), 30 nM (cut thrice), or 240 nM (cut 24 times).
source: Instead, we observe an unchanged kobs, regardless of whether the concentration of ends is 10 nM (cut once), 20 nM (cut twice), 30 nM (cut thrice), or 240 nM (cut 24 times) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown by experiments with restriction-digested plasmid.

claim: Increasing competitor DNA concentrations of plasmid DNA yielded increasing kobs, and the data were best described by global fitting of the kinetic model of Scheme 3 with the formation of a ternary complex.
source: As seen for p18mer, increasing competitor DNA concentrations of plasmid DNA yielded increasing kobs, and the data were best described by global fitting of the kinetic model of Scheme 3 with the formation of a ternary complex (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown by concentration-dependent experiments with plasmid DNA.

claim: The k-2, k3, and k-3 for plasmid DNA are all similar to the values seen previously using p18mer.
source: In fact, the k-2, k3, and k-3 are all similar to the values seen previously using p18mer (Table 1).
evidence: This is shown by comparison of kinetic parameters in Table 1.

claim: There are minimally five binding sites per plasmid.
source: In order to have 5 nM plasmid release all the 25 nM pre-bound p18mer*, we can assume there are minimally five binding sites per plasmid.
evidence: This is inferred from the stoichiometry of the competition experiment.

claim: There are maximally ~450 binding sites per plasmid, estimating that one can place one PARP1 every 10 bp.
source: At the other extreme, estimating that one can place one PARP1 every 10 bp, there are maximally ~450 binding sites.
evidence: This is a theoretical calculation based on DNA length.

claim: The lower limit of the rate of association for plasmid DNA is similar to that measured for p18mer.
source: Interestingly, the lower limit of this rate of association is similar to that measured for p18mer (Table 1), suggesting that undamaged DNA is a very effective competitor of damaged DNA.
evidence: This is concluded from comparison of kinetic parameters.

claim: Intact DNA can engage the monkey-bar mechanism to facilitate the movement of PARP1 around the nucleus.
source: We conclude that intact DNA can also engage the monkey-bar mechanism to facilitate the movement of PARP1 around the nucleus.
evidence: This is concluded from the plasmid competition experiments.

claim: The W589A mutant accumulated to a lower level and with a significantly slower diffusion coefficient than wild-type PARP1 at sites of DNA damage in cells.
source: As seen in Table 2, the W589A mutant accumulated to a lower level and with a significantly slower diffusion coefficient than wild-type PARP1.
evidence: This is shown by laser microirradiation experiments in cells.

claim: The rate of dissociation for W589A from DNA is greater than for wild-type (20 s−1 vs. < 10 s−1).
source: First, the rate of dissociation for W589A from DNA is greater than for wild-type (20 s−1 vs. < 10 s−1).
evidence: This is shown in Table 1.

claim: The apparent KD of W589A for DNA is weaker than that of wild-type PARP1 (5 nM vs. < 3 nM, respectively).
source: Second, the apparent KD of W589A for DNA is weaker than that of wild-type PARP1 (5 nM vs. < 3 nM, respectively).
evidence: This is calculated from the kinetic parameters.

claim: The rate of association of PARP1 with DNA is at or above the commonly accepted diffusion-limited rate of 1–2 nM−1s−1.
source: In vitro, PARP1 binds to DNA at or above the commonly accepted diffusion-limited rate (Record et al., 1991) of 1–2 nM−1s−1, consistent with its extremely rapid accumulation at sites of DNA damage in vivo (Mortusewicz et al., 2007; Aleksandrov et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the measured k1 value and citations to prior literature.

claim: Compared to other model systems using DNA oligomers, PARP1 – DNA association is among the fastest previously reported.
source: In fact, compared to other model systems using DNA oligomers, PARP1 – DNA association is among the fastest previously reported.
evidence: This is supported by comparison to literature values for other proteins.

claim: The rates of association of eukaryotic mismatch repair complex Msh2-Msh6, RNA polymerase, 8-oxoguanine-DNA-glycosylase, and papillomavirus E2 protein with double-stranded DNA are 0.002, 0.004, 0.13, and 0.6–1.4 nM−1s−1, respectively.
source: For comparison, the rates of association of eukaryotic mismatch repair complex Msh2-Msh6 (Biro et al., 2010), RNA polymerase (Johnson and Chester, 1998), 8-oxoguanine-DNA-glycosylase (Lukina et al., 2017), and papillomavirus E2 protein (Ferreiro and de Prat-Gay, 2003) with double-stranded DNA are 0.002, 0.004, 0.13, and 0.6–1.4 nM−1s−1, respectively
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The fast association of PARP1 with DNA means that when dissociation does occur, re-association is most likely to the same site on the same DNA.
source: The fast association of PARP1 with DNA means that when dissociation does occur, re-association is most likely to the same site on the same DNA, as association is faster than diffusion carrying PARP1 away from its original binding site.
evidence: This is an inference from the fast association rate.

claim: PARP1, like other DNA-binding proteins such as transcription factors, must have a mechanism for moving around the genome that does not rely on simple dissociation and re-association.
source: This observation suggests that PARP1, like other DNA-binding proteins such as transcription factors (Mirny et al., 2009), must have a mechanism for moving around the genome that does not rely on simple dissociation and re-association.
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to prior literature on transcription factors.

claim: PARP1 dissociation from DNA is triggered by binding of an additional DNA oligomer or undamaged plasmid prior to dissociation from the first DNA oligomer.
source: Instead, we have found that PARP1 dissociation from DNA is triggered by binding of an additional DNA oligomer or undamaged plasmid prior to dissociation from the first DNA oligomer.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the dissociation experiments.

claim: Undamaged DNA appears to be very effective at promoting the monkey-bar mechanism.
source: Interestingly, undamaged DNA appears to be very effective at promoting the monkey-bar mechanism (Table 1), raising the question of how PARP1 remains stationary at sites of DNA damage.
evidence: This is concluded from the plasmid competition experiments.

claim: The WGR domain provides the other weaker 'hand' to facilitate the movement from one DNA strand to the next.
source: We have found that the WGR domain provides the other weaker 'hand' to facilitate the movement from one DNA strand to the next.
evidence: This is concluded from the domain deletion and point mutation experiments.

claim: Based on the structure of PARP1 bound to a DSB, the WGR domain would need to first dissociate from the bound DNA prior to association with a second different molecule of DNA.
source: Based on the structure of PARP1 bound to a DSB (Langelier et al., 2012), the WGR domain would need to first dissociate from the bound DNA prior to association with a second different molecule of DNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the crystal structure.

claim: An NMR study provides evidence for the stepwise assembly of PARP1 on a site of DNA damage where the Zn1, Zn2, and Zn3 domains engage a DNA molecule prior to final engagement of the WGR and catalytic domains.
source: Such a model is consistent with an NMR study that provides evidence for the stepwise assembly of PARP1 on a site of DNA damage where the Zn1, Zn2, and Zn3 domains engage a DNA molecule prior to final engagement of the WGR and catalytic domains (Eustermann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: A recent study of PARP1 using single-molecule DNA tightrope assays provides strong evidence for a monkey bar mechanism.
source: A recent study of PARP1 using single-molecule DNA tightrope assays provides strong evidence for such a monkey bar mechanism (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Micro-dissociation of one of PARP1's multiple DNA-binding domains from DNA allows it to bind to a free 37 bp fragment, thus preventing rebinding of the domain to the tightrope and accelerating overall macro-dissociation.
source: It was shown that micro-dissociation of one of PARP1's multiple DNA-binding domains from DNA allows it to bind to a free 37 bp fragment, thus preventing rebinding of the domain to the tightrope and accelerating overall macro-dissociation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The mechanism for DNA-dependent DNA dissociation provides a compelling explanation for the wide diversity and significantly weaker dissociation constants previously reported for PARP1 with DNA.
source: Our mechanism for DNA-dependent DNA dissociation also provides a compelling explanation for the wide diversity and significantly weaker dissociation constants previously reported for PARP1 with DNA (Langelier et al., 2018; Clark et al., 2012; Langelier et al., 2010): the measured apparent KD depends strongly on the experimental conditions (i.e. [DNA]) under which the experiment is performed, since higher concentrations of DNA promote release of DNA.
evidence: This is an inference that explains discrepancies in prior literature.

claim: Strong in vitro evidence for a monkey bar mechanism exists for various other proteins, all of them transcription factors.
source: Strong in vitro evidence for a monkey bar mechanism, also known as intersegment transfer, exists for various other proteins, all of them transcription factors.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on transcription factors.

claim: Kinetic experiments have demonstrated strong dependence of DNA release on additional DNA for the lac repressor, cAMP receptor protein and glucocorticoid receptor.
source: Kinetic experiments similar to ours have demonstrated strong dependence of DNA release on additional DNA for the lac repressor (Ruusala and Crothers, 1992), cAMP receptor protein (Fried and Crothers, 1984) and glucocorticoid receptor (Lieberman and Nordeen, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NMR methods have demonstrated that both HoxD9 and Oct1 can bridge one DNA strand to another.
source: NMR methods have demonstrated that both HoxD9 (Iwahara et al., 2006) and Oct1 (Doucleff and Clore, 2008) can bridge one DNA strand to another.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A combination of methods including NMR, rate measurements, and computational modeling have elegantly demonstrated how EgrI uses its three Zn fingers to both bind and scan other DNA fragments as it moves between different recognition sites on different DNA molecules.
source: A combination of methods including NMR, rate measurements, and computational modeling have elegantly demonstrated how EgrI uses its three Zn fingers to both bind and scan other DNA fragments as it moves between different recognition sites on different DNA molecules (Zandarashvili et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Mutagenesis of specific residues in EgrI was used to shift the equilibrium between binding and scanning modes.
source: Interestingly, mutagenesis of specific residues in EgrI was used to shift the equilibrium between binding and scanning modes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The slower accumulation of W589A in cells is a particularly powerful demonstration of the importance of the monkey bar mechanism for PARP1 in finding sites of DNA damage.
source: The slower accumulation of W589A in cells is a particularly powerful demonstration of the importance of the monkey bar mechanism for PARP1 in finding sites of DNA damage for two reasons.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cellular data.

claim: High concentrations of intranuclear DNA allow PARP1 to explore the nucleus rapidly.
source: The monkey bar mechanism provides the explanation for these results: high concentrations of intranuclear DNA allow PARP1 to explore the nucleus rapidly.
evidence: This is an inference from the mechanism and cellular data.

claim: The authors have quantitatively demonstrated the importance of intersegment transfer in the accumulation of a DNA-binding protein at its target destination in vivo.
source: Thus, we have quantitatively demonstrated the importance of intersegment transfer in the accumulation of a DNA-binding protein at its target destination in vivo.
evidence: This is a summary claim of the cellular experiments.

claim: The data showing no effect of four different tight-binding inhibitors of PARP1 on the release of DNA agree with a previous thorough biochemical analysis that also could not find any effects of inhibitors on DNA binding constants or rates of dissociation.
source: Our data showing no effect of four different tight-binding inhibitors of PARP1 on the release of DNA agree with a previous thorough biochemical analysis that also could not find any effects of inhibitors on DNA binding constants or rates of dissociation (Hopkins et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the inhibitor experiments and citation to prior literature.

claim: The mechanistic basis for PARP-trapping is more complex than can be reconstituted in vitro.
source: Thus, the mechanistic basis for PARP-trapping is more complex than can be reconstituted in vitro.
evidence: This is an inference from the lack of effect of inhibitors in vitro.

claim: The results are in agreement with recent findings that PARP inhibitors lead to defective fork recovery and/or homologous recombination-mediated repair, and thus an increase in DNA damage where PARP1 is bound to DNA, and lacking activity due to inhibitor binding.
source: Our results are in agreement with recent findings that PARP inhibitors lead to defective fork recovery and/or homologous recombination-mediated repair, and thus an increase in DNA damage where PARP1 is bound to DNA, and lacking activity due to inhibitor binding (Maya-Mendoza et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent literature.

source: Each construct was also assayed for activity in the presence (+) of NAD+ (200 µM) and one equivalent of p18mer DNA. Higher molecular weight smears are seen for WT and ΔZn2, indicating auto-PARylation.
